title: Festivals and everyday culture
job: Talk about what is happening around you
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE ARTICLE IS THE TENSE HERE. el domingo is THIS Sunday; los domingos is EVERY Sunday. El lunes tengo una cita against Los martes trabajo — one word apart in Spanish, and English needs two different sentences to say the difference at all.

Spanish takes NO preposition with a day. en el domingo is not a sentence: the article alone does the work English hands to on. This is the second half of the same trap, and the half an English speaker builds first.

A date is el + a plain counting number + de + the month: el quince de agosto. Only the first of the month takes an ordinal — el primero, and in Spain simply el uno. L2-M4 already owns primero, so nothing new opens for it here.

Days, months and seasons are written in LOWERCASE: lunes, agosto, verano. The named festivals keep their capitals — Navidad, Nochevieja, Semana Santa — so the habit an English speaker arrives with is right in one place out of two, which is worse than being wrong everywhere.

M8's impersonal se is how a custom gets described: se celebra, se come, se regala. What is done, without saying by whom, is exactly the shape a festival needs — and no new family opens here, these are M8's rows doing their cultural job.

sentences.display: El domingo hay una fiesta en la plaza.
sentences.cue: On Sunday there's a party in the square.
sentences.literal: The Sunday there-is a party in the square.

words.note: A party, and also a public holiday: el lunes es fiesta means nobody works. Feminine, la fiesta, in both senses.

sentences.trap: el domingo means this coming Sunday, once. Nothing here translates on — the article is carrying it.

mistake.display: En el domingo hay una fiesta en la plaza.
mistake.why: Spanish never puts a preposition in front of a day. El domingo already means on Sunday.

sentences.usage: Telling a friend what is on. Neutral; nobody is addressed directly.

sentences.display: Los domingos como en casa. Es mi día favorito.
sentences.cue: On Sundays I eat at home. It's my favourite day.
sentences.literal: The Sundays I-eat in house. It-is my day favourite.

words.note: Masculine despite the -a: el día, los días. It is one of a small set of Greek-derived nouns that break the -a rule, so the article has to be learnt with it.
Favourite, and it follows the noun like almost every Spanish adjective: mi día favorito, never mi favorito día.

sentences.trap: One letter apart from the sentence above and a different meaning: los domingos is every Sunday, as a habit.
sentences.usage: Describing your week. First person, informal enough for a friend and fine anywhere.
sentences.mnemonic: el = this one. los = all of them.

sentences.display: El lunes tengo una cita, y los martes trabajo.
sentences.cue: On Monday I have an appointment, and on Tuesdays I work.
sentences.literal: The Monday I-have an appointment, and the Tuesdays I-work.

words.note: Monday, lowercase. Like martes and viernes it already ends in -s, so only the article moves: el lunes, los lunes.
Tuesday, and unchanged in the plural: los martes. Spanish superstition puts the unlucky day on martes 13, not on a Friday.

sentences.trap: Both halves in one breath: el lunes is one Monday, los martes is every Tuesday. The verb tense does not change at all.
sentences.usage: What you say when someone asks if you are free. cita is M8's word, doing ordinary duty here.

sentences.display: Los miércoles y los jueves estudio en casa.
sentences.cue: On Wednesdays and Thursdays I study at home.
sentences.literal: The Wednesdays and the Thursdays I-study in house.

words.note: Wednesday, stressed on the first syllable: MIÉR-co-les. Another -s day, so the article is what carries the number.
Thursday, the last of the -s days. el jueves is this one; los jueves is all of them.

sentences.trap: Each day needs its own los. Spanish does not let one article stretch across both.
sentences.sound: MIÉR-co-les and JUE-ves both take the stress on the first syllable, against the English habit of the second.

sentences.display: Mi cumpleaños es el quince de agosto. Hay regalos.
sentences.cue: My birthday is the fifteenth of August. There are presents.
sentences.literal: My birthday is the fifteen of August. There-are presents.

words.note: Birthday, already -s in the singular: el cumpleaños, los cumpleaños. It is cumple + años, the years you complete.
Fifteen. A date takes the plain counting number — el quince de agosto — with no ordinal and nothing answering to the English -th.
August, lowercase. Much of Spain shuts in agosto, which is why it is the month a learner hears named most often.
A present, masculine: el regalo. The verb behind it is regalar — to give AS A GIFT, which dar does not say on its own.

sentences.trap: Spanish counts the date: el quince, not el quinceavo. And agosto keeps its small a.

mistake.display: Mi cumpleaños es el quince de Agosto.
mistake.why: Months are lowercase in Spanish. Only the named festivals — Navidad, Nochevieja — take a capital.

sentences.usage: Said about yourself, in any company. es rather than está, because a date is an identity, not a state.

sentences.display: Estamos en verano. Los días son largos.
sentences.cue: It's summer. The days are long.
sentences.literal: We-are in summer. The days are long.

words.note: The we cell of the estar the ladder already taught. Estamos en verano is how Spanish says it is summer: a season is a place you are in.
Summer, lowercase. estamos en verano rather than es verano, because Spanish puts the speaker inside the season.

sentences.trap: Spanish puts you inside the season — estamos en verano — where English uses an empty it is. es verano exists but sounds like a definition.
sentences.usage: Small talk, and the natural opening to anything about the calendar.

sentences.display: En otoño y en invierno hay fiestas.
sentences.cue: In autumn and in winter there are festivals.
sentences.literal: In autumn and in winter there-are festivals.

words.note: Autumn, lowercase, with the ñ of mañana. South of the equator it lands at the opposite end of the year, and the word does not change.
Winter, lowercase. en invierno is the frame; an article appears only when one particular winter is meant.

sentences.trap: No article with a season after en: en invierno, not en el invierno, unless you mean one particular winter.
sentences.usage: Describing the year where you live. Neutral, and it claims nothing about any one region.

sentences.display: Se celebra la Semana Santa en primavera.
sentences.cue: Holy Week is celebrated in spring.
sentences.literal: One-celebrates the Holy Week in spring.

words.note: M8's impersonal se with celebrar, the standard verb for a festival. Indexed whole, so L2-M4's bare se keeps its own row.
The week before Easter, capitalised because it is a name. In Spain it means processions; in much of Latin America it means a week at the coast.
Spring, lowercase and feminine: la primavera. en primavera takes no article at all.

sentences.trap: The season is lowercase and the festival is not. Both rules are in one short sentence, pulling opposite ways.
sentences.usage: How a custom is described to someone who does not know it. No person is named, which is the point of se.

sentences.display: En diciembre se come mucho, y se regala algo en Navidad.
sentences.cue: In December people eat a lot, and something is given at Christmas.
sentences.literal: In December one-eats much, and one-gives-as-gift something in Christmas.

words.note: December, lowercase — unlike the Navidad that sits inside it, the month takes no capital.
How a custom around food is stated: en diciembre se come mucho. Indexed whole, like se celebra, so the bare se is untouched.
regalar under M8's impersonal se: what people give, rather than what you gave. Indexed whole for the same reason as se come.
Christmas, capitalised as a name. In Spain the presents often wait for Reyes on 6 January rather than arriving on the 25th.

sentences.trap: se come and se regala name no one at all. Adding a subject — la gente come — turns a custom into a report about particular people.
sentences.usage: What you say about your own December to someone from elsewhere. It claims the custom for nobody in particular, which is honest.

sentences.display: En Nochevieja hay una feria en la plaza.
sentences.cue: On New Year's Eve there's a fair in the square.
sentences.literal: In New-Year's-Eve there-is a fair in the square.

words.note: New Year's Eve — literally old night. The twelve grapes at midnight belong to it. Christmas Eve is a different word, Nochebuena.
A town's annual fair, with music, food and a fairground. Andalusia's are the famous ones; further north the same event is often a verbena.

sentences.trap: A festival takes en — en Nochevieja, en Navidad — while a day takes nothing at all. The two rules sit side by side and are not the same.
sentences.usage: A local fact, said locally. feria is a Spanish word for a Spanish thing; elsewhere the same night has other names.
